## Everyone has a camera

<!-- ~50 sec -->

Your phone takes photos that once needed professional gear.

. . .

::: {.big-statement}
So why do people still pay photographers?
:::

. . .

The camera was never the skill. Knowing what's worth shooting, and whether the
image is real, is.

. . .

Analytics is the same. Everyone has the camera now: dashboards, models, AI.

::: {.notes}
Soften the "15 years ago" claim from the old draft; "once needed professional gear"
is safe and doesn't invite a debate about camera specs. Everyone in the room loves
analytics, so the point isn't "you're wrong," it's "the camera isn't the skill."
Deliver it as an observation, not a challenge.
:::

## Three tests {.center}

<!-- ~30 sec -->

::: {.big-statement}
**Framing:** does it change a decision?<br>
**Noise:** is it signal or luck?<br>
**The client:** is someone empowered to act on it?
:::

::: {.notes}
Use one club to show all three: Liverpool. Say it once here, return to it in the
close. "Noise" is a literal word in both photography and statistics, which is why
it's the strongest of the three labels.
:::

# Framing {background-color="#1b5635"}

<!-- ~60 sec -->

Liverpool needed a new manager.

. . .

Ian Graham, their director of research, looked at Borussia Dortmund.

. . .

The league table said Dortmund had a disappointing stretch. The data said they
were still the **second-best team in Germany**, and among the **unluckiest** over

. . .

Same league table. Different frame. And the result was a hiring decision, not a report.

# Noise {background-color="#1b5635"}

## A striker is 9-for-10 on penalties

<!-- ~45 sec -->

**It's a shootout Saturday. Is he your designated taker?**

. . .

Raw math says 90%. Your gut says *"...it's ten kicks."*

. . .

Ten kicks is a grainy photo. You can't tell a face from a smudge.

. . .

What helps is what you already know about what you're looking at:
[penalties go in about three in four times]{.placeholder}. That's a **prior**.

::: {.notes}
Setup only. The tension: the raw number is the only thing on screen, but you carry
two pieces of information, the league rate and his ten kicks. Bayesian statistics
is the rule for combining them.
:::

## Prior + evidence = posterior

<!-- ~75 sec -->

$$
\theta \sim \text{Beta}(31,\,9) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta \mid \text{9 makes, 1 miss} \sim \text{Beta}(40,\,10)
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
a0 <- 31; b0 <- 9            # illustrative prior: ~77% average, worth ~40 kicks
made <- 9; n <- 10
a1 <- a0 + made; b1 <- b0 + (n - made)
x     <- seq(0.4, 1, length.out = 500)
prior <- dbeta(x, a0, b0)
post  <- dbeta(x, a1, b1)
p_better <- 1 - pbeta(a0 / (a0 + b0), a1, b1)
plot(x, post, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#C68346",
     xlab = "True penalty conversion rate", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     ylim = c(0, max(prior, post) * 1.1), cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
lines(x, prior, lwd = 4, col = "#1b5635", lty = 2)
abline(v = 0.90, lty = 3, lwd = 2)
text(0.90, max(prior, post) * 0.9, "Raw: 90%", pos = 2, cex = 1.2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 1.2, lwd = 4,
       col = c("#1b5635", "#C68346"), lty = c(2, 1),
       legend = c("Prior (league-level belief)",
                  paste0("Posterior (mean ~", round(100 * a1 / (a1 + b1)), "%)")))
mtext(paste0("P(better than average) = ", round(p_better, 2)),
      side = 3, line = 0, cex = 1.1)
```

. . .

The update is addition: 31 + 9 makes, 9 + 1 miss. And the answer is a **distribution**,
so you can ask: *how likely is he actually better than average?*

::: {.notes}
Prior Beta(31, 9), mean 77.5%, worth about 40 kicks. Posterior Beta(40, 10), mean
80%. A decision-maker doesn't need "80%." They need "two in three odds he's better
than average, and here's how much to trust that." A point estimate can't give you that.
:::

## The prior is an assumption, said out loud

<!-- ~60 sec -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
priors <- list(`Weak prior`     = c(3.1, 0.9),
               `Moderate prior` = c(31, 9),
               `Strong prior`   = c(77.5, 22.5))
cols <- c("#C68346", "#1b5635", "#6a6a6a")
ltys <- c(1, 2, 3)
obs  <- list(c(9, 10), c(90, 100))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 1, 3, 1))
for (d in obs) {
  x  <- seq(0.5, 1, length.out = 500)
  ys <- lapply(priors, function(p) dbeta(x, p[1] + d[1], p[2] + d[2] - d[1]))
  plot(x, ys[[1]], type = "l", lwd = 3, col = cols[1], lty = ltys[1],
       xlab = "True conversion rate", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
       ylim = c(0, max(unlist(ys)) * 1.1), cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1,
       main = paste0(d[1], " of ", d[2], " kicks"), cex.main = 1.3)
  for (i in 2:3) lines(x, ys[[i]], lwd = 3, col = cols[i], lty = ltys[i])
  if (d[2] == 10) legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 1.0, lwd = 3,
                         col = cols, lty = ltys, legend = names(priors))
}
```

. . .

With ten kicks, your assumption matters. With a hundred, the data takes over.
More exposures sharpen the picture.

. . .

Every model has a prior. A model that doesn't show you one is still using it.

::: {.notes}
Weak prior is worth about 4 kicks, moderate about 40, strong about 100. The usual
objection to Bayes is "isn't the prior just your opinion?" Answer: yes, and it is
stated, adjustable, and overwhelmed by evidence. This sets up the NBA project:
thousands of players is the right-hand panel.
:::

## My own project: does pedigree predict a longer NBA career?

<!-- ~75 sec -->

*With Jonas Schiel.* "Blue blood" programs: Duke, North Carolina, UCLA, Indiana,
Kentucky, Kansas.

. . .

Career length is a count, right-skewed. Model: **Poisson likelihood, Gamma prior.**
Prior expectation: about 5 years for blue-blood alumni, about 3.5 for everyone else.

. . .

Same logic as the penalties. Different conjugate pair, much more data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 9
lo  <- c(5.09, 4.27); hi <- c(5.51, 4.40)
par(mar = c(4.5, 10, 1, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(3.8, 6), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     xlab = "Mean career length (years), 95% credible interval", ylab = "",
     cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
segments(lo, c(2, 1), hi, c(2, 1), lwd = 10, col = c("#C68346", "#1b5635"), lend = 1)
axis(2, at = c(2, 1), labels = c("Blue-blood alumni", "Everyone else"),
     las = 1, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 1.2)
```

::: {.notes}
Numbers from your write-up: 95% CI for mean career length (5.09, 5.51) vs (4.27,
4.40); difference (0.74, 1.19). Likely questions:
(1) "Didn't you pick different priors for each group?" Yes (5 vs 3.5 years). With
this much data the intervals are driven by the data, but the cleanest answer is a
sensitivity check: refit with the SAME prior for both groups and report that the
conclusion holds. Do this before you present if you can; it turns a vulnerability
into the strongest slide.
(2) "Is Poisson right?" Poisson forces variance = mean and allows zero years; real
careers are overdispersed and at least one year. Say you treated it as a known
simplification (your write-up already does) and that a negative binomial or
zero-truncated model would be the next step.
:::

## What the model can and can't say

<!-- ~60 sec -->

| Career longer than | Blue-blood | Everyone else |
|:------------------:|:----------:|:-------------:|
| 5 years            | **42.8%**  | 27.1%         |
| 10 years           | 1.8%       | 0.76%         |

. . .

There's a real gap: the 95% credible interval for the difference is 0.74 to 1.19 years.

. . .

What I can't say: that the **school** causes it. Top prospects pick top programs.
And the model treats each season as independent, which careers aren't.

. . .

::: {.big-statement}
Knowing what your model can't say is part of the model.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the "Noise" test applied to your own work: a real, quantified difference,
reported with its limits. Next step you named in the write-up: control for draft
position, era, and position; or update the blue-blood definition (UCLA). If asked
"so does it matter?": it predicts, it doesn't prove cause.
:::

## The math behind a "safe" bet

<!-- ~60 sec -->

| Typical line | Win on a \$100 bet | Break-even win rate |
|:------------:|:------------------:|:-------------------:|
| -110         | \$90.91            | **52.4%**           |

. . .

$$
EV = 0.50 \times (+90.91) + 0.50 \times (-100) = -\$4.55
$$

per \$100 bet, **on average, forever** -- even on a true coin flip.

::: {.notes}
Math is exact. Don't moralize; let the number be the point.
:::

# Backup {background-color="#6a6a6a"}

## What predicts an NHL player's plus-minus?

<!-- Backup: Q&A / interviews -->

*With Claire Peterson and Anzlei Larsen.* Multiple linear regression, 1,000-iteration
cross-validation, NHL seasons 2000-01 to 2024-25.

. . .

**Adjusted R² = 0.123.** Cross-validated RMSE 0.157, effectively unbiased.

. . .

We reported 12% as the finding, not the failure. Hockey is noisy, and the variables
that probably matter (team quality, age, coaching system) weren't in the data.

::: {.notes}
Shooting percentage had the strongest positive association, then position
(defensemen and centers), assists, and shots per game. Interactive explorer:
nhl-explorer.streamlit.app. Interview use: "I know what my model can't do, and I say so."
:::

## Do it for the whole squad

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(7)
N     <- 150
theta <- rbeta(N, 31, 9)                  # each player's true rate (simulated)
n     <- sample(3:30, N, replace = TRUE)  # kicks taken: some players have very few
made  <- rbinom(N, n, theta)
raw   <- made / n
shr   <- (31 + made) / (40 + n)
rmse  <- function(e) sqrt(mean((e - theta)^2))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(theta, raw, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#C68346", 0.6), cex = 1.1,
     xlim = c(0.5, 1), ylim = c(0.2, 1),
     xlab = "True rate", ylab = "Estimated rate", cex.lab = 1.2,
     main = paste0("Raw rate (error ", round(rmse(raw), 3), ")"), cex.main = 1.2)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
plot(theta, shr, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#1b5635", 0.6), cex = 1.1,
     xlim = c(0.5, 1), ylim = c(0.2, 1),
     xlab = "True rate", ylab = "", cex.lab = 1.2,
     main = paste0("With a prior (error ", round(rmse(shr), 3), ")"), cex.main = 1.2)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

Players with 3 kicks and players with 30 shouldn't be trusted equally. Shrink each
estimate in proportion to how little you know.

::: {.notes}
Simulated; we know the true rates so we can score the estimates. Partial pooling in
its simplest form. In practice the prior's parameters are estimated from the whole
population (empirical Bayes) or modeled hierarchically.
:::

## The same team, 10,000 seasons

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(42)
p   <- c(win = 0.30, draw = 0.27, loss = 0.43)   # illustrative mid-table team
pts <- replicate(10000, { r <- rmultinom(1, 38, p); 3 * r[1] + r[2] })
ci  <- quantile(pts, c(0.05, 0.95))
hist(pts, breaks = seq(min(pts) - 0.5, max(pts) + 0.5, 1),
     col = "#C68346", border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = "Season points (38 games)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n",
     cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
abline(v = 38 * (3 * p["win"] + p["draw"]), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "#1b5635")
abline(v = ci, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 1.2,
       legend = paste0("90% of seasons: ", ci[1], " to ", ci[2], " points"))
```

Identical team. Identical strength. The only thing that changed was luck.

::: {.notes}
Backup for "what does unlucky mean." Illustrative win/draw/loss probabilities for a
middling team; say so.
:::
